citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume countable choice. Let $H_0$ be a separable real Hilbert space with a complete orthonormal basis indexed by the disjoint union of a finite set $I_*$ and the level indices $(\ell,k)$ with $\ell\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^\ell$. Write the basis vectors as $(e_i)_{i\in I_*}$ and $(e_{\ell k})$. For $r\ge0$, define
$$H_r:=\left\{x\in H_0:\sum_{i\in I_*}|\langle x,e_i\rangle_{H_0}|^2+\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{2r\ell}\sum_{k<2^\ell}|\langle x,e_{\ell k}\rangle_{H_0}|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with inner product given by the corresponding weighted coefficient sum and norm squared
$$\|x\|_{H_r}^2:=\sum_{i\in I_*}|\langle x,e_i\rangle_{H_0}|^2+\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{2r\ell}\sum_{k<2^\ell}|\langle x,e_{\ell k}\rangle_{H_0}|^2.$$
Then $H_r$ is a separable real Hilbert space. Its displayed basis is complete and orthogonal in $H_r$, with squared basis norms $1$ on the finite family and $2^{2r\ell}$ on level $\ell$, and the inclusion $H_r\hookrightarrow H_0$ is continuous with operator norm at most $1$.

Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be separable real Hilbert spaces with a continuous inclusion $H_1\hookrightarrow H_0$. Let $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be an orthonormal basis of $H_0$ that is a complete orthogonal basis of $H_1$, write $w_j=\|e_j\|_{H_1}^2>0$, and set $f_j=e_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, so $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ is an orthonormal basis of $H_1$. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be independent real random variables on one probability space with $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$, and let $\lambda_j\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j<\infty$. Then
$$S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,\xi_j e_j$$
converges almost surely in $H_1$ and in $L^2(\Omega;H_1)$ to an $H_1$-valued Borel-measurable random element $S$, with
$$\mathbb E\|S\|_{H_1}^2=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jw_j.$$
These norm-convergence conclusions use no choice axiom beyond the supplied probability space and variables. For the following Gaussian conclusions, assume in addition that each $\xi_j$ has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. Under the Axiom of Choice and countable choice, $S$ is a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $H_1$. Its covariance map $C:H_1^*\to H_1$, transported to $H_1$ by the Hilbert-space Riesz identification, is diagonal in the basis $(f_j)_{j\ge1}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_jw_j$, and these eigenvalues are summable. If $D$ is a Borel forward-map domain in $H_1$ and $\mathbb P(S\in D)=1$, then the law of $S$ is a prior on $D$. Under the Axiom of Choice there is $a>0$ such that
$$\mathbb E\exp\!\bigl(a\|S\|_{H_1}^2\bigr)<\infty.$$

Let $X$ be a specified real separable Banach or Hilbert parameter space with metric $d_X(x,x')=\|x-x'\|_X$ and its norm topology. Let $(Y,d_Y)$ be a metric data space equipped with a sigma-algebra $\Sigma_Y$, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth set, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map. Choose a Borel set $D\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $D\subseteq U$ such that the restriction $G:=F|_D:D\to Y$ is measurable for the trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. A prior on this forward domain is a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ such that $\mu(D)=1$. Its restriction $\mu|_D$, defined by $\mu|_D(A)=\mu(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$, is then a probability measure on $D$, and the induced data law is $G_\#(\mu|_D)$, defined by $G_\#(\mu|_D)(E)=(\mu|_D)(G^{-1}(E))$ for $E\in\Sigma_Y$. A Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu(D)<1$ is not a prior on this declared forward domain.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.
IID square-integrable real variables satisfy $S_n/n\to\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ (Dense, nowhere dense and codense subsets of a topological space, and the criterion by basic open sets, Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

derivations.claim: Let $H_0=L^2([0,1])$. By [F1] under countable choice [A2], it is a real Hilbert space. The complete basis [F10] has a countable index set, so its finite rational linear combinations form a countable set. Its finite real linear span is dense by [F10], and approximating each finite list of real coefficients by rationals makes the rational span dense as well. Hence $H_0$ is separable by [F11]. Enumerate the finite scaling family first and the detail wavelets by increasing $\ell$ and then $k$, set $\lambda_i=0$ on the scaling family, and set $\lambda_{\ell k}=2^{-2\ell(s+1/2)}$ and $w_j=1$ on detail levels. Then $\sum_j\lambda_jw_j=\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^\ell2^{-2\ell(s+1/2)}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{-2s\ell}<\infty$ because $s>0$. Apply [F3] under AC and countable choice [A1]–[A2] to obtain the Borel centered Gaussian limit $W$ in $H_0$. The identity on $D=H_0$ is measurable and $\mathbb P(W\in D)=1$, so [F4] makes its law a prior on $D$.

Enumerate the detail coefficients by increasing level and then by $k$, write the corresponding standard normals as $(\eta_n)_{n\ge1}$, and set $Z_n=\eta_n^2$. By [F9] under countable choice [A2], the square map is measurable. Since each $\eta_n$ has the same standard normal law, the $Z_n$ have the same pushforward law under this map; [F6] preserves independence, so [F7] makes $(Z_n)$ IID. By [F5] under AC [A1], their mean is $1$ and their variance is finite; [F8] gives $R_N/N\to1$ almost surely for $R_N=\sum_{n=1}^NZ_n$. For every $\ell\ge0$, set $A_\ell=2^{-\ell}\sum_{k<2^\ell}\xi_{\ell k}^2$. For $\ell\ge1$, put $N_\ell=2^\ell-1$, so $A_\ell=(R_{N_{\ell+1}}-R_{N_\ell})/2^\ell$. Since $N_{\ell+1}/2^\ell\to2$ and $N_\ell/2^\ell\to1$ as $\ell\to\infty$, the strong-law limits give $A_\ell\to2-1=1$ almost surely for the same variables used in step 1.1.

Fix $0\le r<s$ and take $H_1=B^r_{2,2}([0,1])$. By [F2], it is a separable Hilbert space continuously included in $H_0$, with basis weights $1$ on the finite scaling family and $w_{\ell k}=2^{2r\ell}$ on detail levels. The weighted eigenvalue sum is $\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^\ell2^{-2\ell(s+1/2)}2^{2r\ell}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{-2(s-r)\ell}<\infty$. Apply [F3] under AC and countable choice [A1]–[A2] to the same coefficients as in step 1.1; the partial wavelet sums converge almost surely in $H_1$. Their $H_0$ limit is $W$ by step 1.1, and continuity of the inclusion makes the $H_1$ limit the same element. Hence $W\in B^r_{2,2}([0,1])$ almost surely for this fixed $r$.

For each detail wavelet, its coordinate functional is continuous on $H_0$; after the term enters the partial sums, the coefficient is $2^{-\ell(s+1/2)}\xi_{\ell k}$, so convergence in step 1.1 gives the same coefficient for $W$. The scaling coefficients vanish by construction. Therefore $\|W\|_{B^s_{2,2}}^2=\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{2\ell s}\sum_{k<2^\ell}2^{-2\ell(s+1/2)}\xi_{\ell k}^2=\sum_{\ell\ge0}A_\ell$. By step 2.1, $A_\ell\to1$ almost surely, so the nonnegative series diverges and $W\notin B^s_{2,2}([0,1])$ almost surely.
